IAM: roles, trust, and least privilege on your autoscaler policy

One sitting (about 30 minutes, plus a 20-minute reading). One win: you can say exactly what your Ray autoscaler is allowed to do, and what it shouldn't be.

Why this lesson

Your training fleet already runs on IAM you built by hand: a role the workers use to reach S3 and ECR (#97), and a policy that lets the Ray autoscaler launch and kill instances. Before Terraform adopts them (#141, #142), you should be able to read each one and say what it allows. One of them allows more than it needs to, and finding that is this lesson's rep.

The placement showed you already know the basics (the IAM question was right first try), so this lesson moves fast through the vocabulary and spends its time on your real policies.

Vim tip (1 minute, optional)

Change inside quotes: ci". It deletes the text between a pair of double quotes and puts you in Insert mode. The catch: if the cursor isn't inside a quoted string, Vim picks the first quoted string on the line. On "Resource": "*" with the cursor at the start, ci" changes "Resource", not "*".

So jump first: $ (end of line, inside "*"), then ci", type the new value, <Esc>. Example: turning "*" into "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*" is $ci"arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*<Esc>. You'll edit a lot of policy JSON this course.

Optional: paste the keys you'd use (or a vim -W recording) to change "*" to "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*" on the line "Resource": "*", starting with the cursor at the start of the line.

Not graded. Replay with python3 scripts/vimcheck.py --drill topics/swe/vim-drills.json v04-ciq "<keys>" and reply with the result.

Before the lesson: reading (about 20 minutes)

Reading

Stephane Maarek, Ultimate AWS Certified Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03), slides (your course, in your library):

  1. The "AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM)" section, from "IAM: Users & Groups" through "IAM Guidelines & Best Practices". The slides that matter most: "IAM Policies Structure" and "IAM Roles for Services".
  2. In the advanced identity section, the four slides "IAM Conditions" (both), "IAM for S3", and "IAM Policy Evaluation Logic". Skip the Organizations and SCP slides before them.

The lesson restates everything it uses, so it works if you only skim.

In your own words: what's the difference between an IAM user and an IAM role, and why do EC2 instances get a role rather than access keys?

Got it: a user is a long-lived identity for a person (password and/or long-term access keys); a role has no long-term credentials and is assumed by someone or something it trusts, getting temporary credentials. Instances use a role (through an instance profile) so no keys sit in code, images or config, and the credentials rotate automatically.

Part 1: what a role is, using your own (8 minutes)

A policy is a JSON document of statements: each has an Effect (Allow or Deny), an Action list, a Resource list, and an optional Condition. A role is an identity with two kinds of policy attached:

The trust policy: who may become this role. Your RayClusterS3Role (#97) trusts one principal: the EC2 service. ``json {"Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com"}, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"} `` Nothing else can assume it: not you, not Lambda, not another account.

The permissions policies: what the role may do once assumed. Two: an inline policy allowing s3:PutObject, GetObject, DeleteObject and ListBucket on your one bucket (not AmazonS3FullAccess), and AWS's managed AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly.

The instance profile: how EC2 carries it. EC2 doesn't attach a role directly; it attaches an instance profile, a container holding one role. RayEC2Profile holds RayClusterS3Role, and deploy/ray-cluster.yaml names the profile. Forget add-role-to-instance-profile and the nodes get a profile with no permissions at all (the pitfall #97 warns about).

One more permission links them. Whoever launches an instance with a role must be allowed to hand over that role: iam:PassRole. That's why the autoscaler's policy (Part 3) has a PassOwnRoleToWorkers statement. Without that check, anyone who could launch an instance could give it any role, including an admin one.

For your training fleet, which document answers each question?

Trust = who may become the role; permissions = what the role may do; the instance profile is how EC2 carries one role; PassRole is a permission of the launcher, not of the role being passed.

A teammate edits RayClusterS3Role's trust policy to trust lambda.amazonaws.com instead of ec2.amazonaws.com. What breaks?

The EC2 service assumes the role on the instance's behalf. Once the trust policy stops trusting EC2, that assumption fails, and every permission behind it (S3 and ECR alike) is gone for the workers.

Part 2: how AWS decides (7 minutes)

Every API call is checked against all the policies that apply. The rule, from AWS's "policy evaluation logic":

  1. Default deny. Nothing is allowed unless some policy allows it.
  2. An explicit Allow makes it allowed...
  3. ...unless any policy has an explicit Deny for it. An explicit deny always wins.

And resources are named by ARN. One S3 trap the reading shows: s3:ListBucket acts on the bucket (arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket), while object actions act on objects (arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*). That's why #97's policy lists both ARNs.

A role has one policy allowing s3:* on the training bucket and another policy denying s3:DeleteObject on arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*. A worker calls DeleteObject on a checkpoint in that bucket. What happens?

Order and breadth don't matter: any explicit Deny that matches wins. That's what makes a deny a reliable guard rail.

Which resource ARN does each action need in the policy?

Listing is a bucket-level action; reading, writing and deleting act on objects. Give ListBucket only the /* ARN and listing fails.

Part 3: least privilege on the autoscaler's policy (10 minutes)

This is deploy/iam/ray-autoscaler-policy.json in 3dChessRLAgent, the policy the Ray head uses to manage workers:

``json {"Sid": "RayAutoscalerEc2", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["ec2:RunInstances", "ec2:TerminateInstances", "ec2:CreateTags", "ec2:DescribeInstances", "ec2:DescribeInstanceTypes", "ec2:DescribeImages"], "Resource": "*"}, {"Sid": "PassOwnRoleToWorkers", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "iam:PassRole", "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:role/RayClusterS3Role"} ``

What's already good. PassRole names exactly one role. The autoscaler can't hand workers anything stronger than RayClusterS3Role.

What's too broad. ec2:TerminateInstances on "*" lets the Ray head terminate any instance in the account: a bug in the autoscaler, or anyone who gets onto the head node, could kill machines that have nothing to do with training.

What can be scoped, and how. Ray tags every instance it launches with ray-cluster-name (your cluster_name is chess-rl; the key is in Ray's autoscaler/tags.py). IAM can check a resource's tags: a condition like "StringEquals": {"ec2:ResourceTag/ray-cluster-name": "chess-rl"} limits termination to your cluster's own nodes.

What can't be scoped. The Describe* actions don't support resource-level permissions; they need "*". They only read, so that's acceptable.

The subtle one: CreateTags. AWS lets you allow tagging only during launch (condition ec2:CreateAction = RunInstances). But Ray also re-tags running nodes as their status changes. Allow tagging only at launch and the autoscaler breaks. So tagging needs two allowances: at launch, and on instances already tagged chess-rl. This is the kind of thing a least-privilege review has to check against how the software actually behaves.

For the autoscaler's policy, how should each action's Resource be handled?

Terminate is destructive and supports tag conditions, so it's the one to fix first. Describe calls only read and can't be scoped. PassRole is already as narrow as it gets.

You scope ec2:CreateTags with the condition ec2:CreateAction = RunInstances and nothing else. What goes wrong with Ray?

The condition allows tagging only inside the launch call. Ray also changes tags (like node status) on nodes that are already running, and those CreateTags calls would now be denied.

Required rep (the next tech-lane lesson waits for it)

3dChessRLAgent #142, the "least-privilege IAM review" part. #142 imports this policy into Terraform, so review it first. Post a comment on #142 that decides:

  1. which actions get a tag condition, and on which tag;
  2. how CreateTags stays working for Ray (launch-time and running nodes);
  3. whether RunInstances should require the ray-cluster-name tag on new instances (aws:RequestTag), and the cost of doing so;
  4. whether to also pin the region (aws:RequestedRegion), given the single-AZ design in #143.

You decide; I write the JSON and the Terraform from your decisions. Ship = the comment's link, pasted here. Skipping is fine with a reason.

Paste the link to your #142 comment when it's up (or a reason for skipping).
